name: Bank reconciliation
seoTitle: Bank reconciliation Calculator — Formula, Units & Example
seoDesc: Bank reconciliation: work out cash book balance from the automatic bank payments and the bank charges. A free finance calculator with the formula, units…
summary: Supply the automatic bank payments, the bank charges, the NSF cheques and the interest earned and the Bank reconciliation calculator solves for cash book balance. Think of it as a shortcut for a budget, a loan conversation, a payslip check or a what-if before you talk to a lender. Nothing is submitted anywhere: the arithmetic runs in the page you are looking at.

sections.title: How does the Bank reconciliation calculator work?
sections.html:
The Bank reconciliation calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports cash book balance in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the automatic bank payments, the bank charges, the NSF cheques and the interest earned.

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Bank reconciliation calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Cash book balance=automatic bank payments + bank charges + adjusted ending balance − interest earned + NSF cheques − receivable
Adjusted ending balance=bank balance + deposit in transit − unpresented cheques
Unreconciled difference=the absolute value of (adjusted ending balance − adjusted ending balance)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Take NSF cheques = 0, Bank balance = 10, Deposit in transit = 10 and Unpresented cheques = 10. The calculator returns Adjusted ending balance = 10.

The point of the example is the scale, not the particular digits: swap in your own figures and the same relationship produces your answer.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Adjusted ending balance = 10 should be roughly the size you expected from NSF cheques = 0 and Bank balance = 10.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Bank reconciliation calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Sizing up a purchase before you commit to it
  • Preparing questions for a lender, an accountant or an adviser
  • Building a monthly budget and testing how one number shifts the rest
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the automatic bank payments, the bank charges and the NSF cheques — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Bank reconciliation calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns cash book balance, derived from the automatic bank payments, the bank charges and the NSF cheques. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Bank reconciliation calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the automatic bank payments, the bank charges, the NSF cheques and the interest earned, which is 9 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter cash book balance in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Cash book balance opens in US Dollar and the chip beside it offers 113 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Adjusted ending balance = 10. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Bank reconciliation calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
